Tune in at 4:40 p.m. ET as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy joins CNBC TV to discuss the certification. Watch in real time on CNBC+ or the CNBC Pro stream. The 737 Max 10, the largest model in the family, was set to start flying in 2020, but increased scrutiny following two Max crashes in 2018 and 2019 and other safety issues delayed its certification. Engineering changes were also required, including to an anti-icing system for the aircraft's engines. "The FAA's decision follows a thorough review of the aircraft's design and safety requirements," said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. "We will continue to hold Boeing to the highest safety standards." CEO Kelly Ortberg said at a Morgan Stanley conference on Sept. 16 that orders for the aircraft make up about 30% of Boeing's backlog. Customers include Alaska Airlines , American Airlines , United Airlines and Delta Air Lines . The world's richest person appeared to suggest that he would use the Trump Account program to make this historic gift. Tierney L. Cross | The Washington Post | Getty Images Elon Musk said on Monday that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. He appeared to suggest the gift could land in Trump Accounts — thanking Brad Gerstner, an architect of the program, for "helping enable this" in a comment on X . Posts from the White House and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also referenced Musk's gift as benefiting Trump Accounts. But if the shares are distributed through the new investment accounts for children, the gift could come with significant strings attached. Musk's announcement comes weeks after the U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out guidelines for stock donations to Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts. Those include restrictions on selling donated stock: Children who receive it generally cannot sell for five years, even if the company runs into financial trouble. Treasury's temporary regulations, subject to revision after public comment, aim to encourage stock gifts. But they also give donors unusual influence over children's investments, according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC. Under the new Trump Account rules, however, it's "the donor that's dictating the terms of the gift," she said. Representatives for Musk, Gerstner and the Treasury Department did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the proposed gift. According to the Treasury, about 70 million Trump Accounts have been created, including more than 60 million through a recent auto-enrollment effort . Trump Accounts are available to all children with U.S. citizenship under age 18 with valid Social Security numbers. Musk would be the second philanthropist to publicly announce a stock pledge to Trump Accounts: SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell pledged earlier this summer to use the Trump Account program to gift some 2 million shares . That gift has not yet been distributed. What stock sale restrictions mean for children Trump Account beneficiaries do not have the latitude to sell under circumstances that other investors might otherwise. Under the new rules, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17. Before then, early sales are permitted only in limited circumstances, such as certain corporate transitions or when the stock is formally delisted from a national securities exchange — not when financial or legal problems emerge that might prompt an investor to sell. "Giving families more choices and more ability to hold the assets that they think are best for them and their kids' future ... would be a good thing," said Adam Michel, director of tax policy studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank. "But this is not really that, because you have no choice in the asset that is being deposited into your child's account, and then you also have no ability to sell it for the five-year holding period." watch now VIDEO 1:53 01:53 Elon Musk vows to donate SpaceX shares to every child in America The Exchange The temporary regulations also mandate that if any gifted stock is sold too early, the trustee must purchase the same number and class of shares "as soon as practicable." This increases beneficiaries' risk of loss if the share price rises before the trustee repurchases the stock, according to Schenck. Beneficiaries would ultimately bear that cost. "If the fiduciary makes an investment mistake, then the focus is typically restoring value to the beneficiary. But here, the focus seems to be restoring the specific security itself," said Schenck, who left the IRS in 2025 for law firm Caplin & Drysdale. CNBC has learned the buyback provision is intended to quickly correct trading errors, though the regulations do not explicitly state that purpose or limit the requirement to accidental sales. Donor incentives behind the holding rule The temporary regulations cite donor interests. According to the text, "Donors are attracted by the hope that a stock contribution with a five-year holding period may lead recipients and their families to feel that they have a stake in the fate of the corporation." headlines.article_text: Mike Bloomberg spent $80M to boost Democrats in midterms: NYT Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Former New York Mayor Mike Bloomberg spent $80 million in September and October to help Democratic candidates in November's midterm elections, The New York Times reported. The billionaire's contributions are part of a Democratic effort to regain majority control of the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterm elections. President Donald Trump has vowed to spend $400 million to help Republican candidates this election cycle. Former Mayor of New York City Mike Bloomberg speaks at the opening session of the Qatar Economic Forum 2025 in Doha, Qatar, on May 20, 2025. Noushad Thekkayil | Nurphoto | Getty Images Mike Bloomberg spent $80 million in September and October to help Democrats regain majority control of the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterm elections, The New York Times reported Tuesday, citing his team. Shortly after The Times published its article about Bloomberg's campaign spending, his fellow billionaire, President Donald Trump , in a social media post reiterated his vow to spend $400 million to boost Republican candidates. The dueling announcements came as Republicans are increasingly worried about retaining their majorities in both chambers of Congress. Many political analysts expect Democrats to win control of the House, and multiple polls show Democrats within reach of winning a majority of seats in the Senate. Bloomberg "is of the view that resources matter in campaigns," his political advisor Howard Wolfson told The Times. Bloomberg, a former New York City mayor, "expects a result," Wolfson said. With the $80 million in spending, Bloomberg is among the top five largest individual Democratic donors according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings for the 2025-2026 election cycle. Wolfson did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Before Tuesday's announcement, Bloomberg was known to have donated $23 million to Democrats and affiliated causes this election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission records through Tuesday. As of the beginning of October, Bloomberg had put $11 million behind a super PAC supporting Micah Lasher in New York's 12th Congressional District and $2.5 million toward Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's reelection, according to campaign-finance records . Trump promised that his spending will top $400 million by Election Day, Nov. 3. FEC filings as of Tuesday afternoon so far show roughly $200 million in identifiable spending and ad reservations tied to Trump's political operation, leaving a gap between what's publicly visible and Trump's broader claim. In September, Trump said he had " close to a billion dollars " in his super PAC, MAGA Inc., and planned to spend $400 million to $500 million on the midterms.
